items.title: Ray Conniff interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 14, 1998
items.q: And you know Justin Sogg and all them people were around

ctx.x: You didn’t get three percent of what they were actually selling it for. You got three percent of just the record.

The record itself — oh there were a lot of other little clauses. Like they used to be made of, what was it, acetate? They used to break. They had a ten percent breakage clause in there. You know the breakage clause is still in all the contracts? There is nothing that can break anymore. Now they say it’s because of the stuff that comes back or something. But anyway, yeah, you got three percent. Oh there were a lot of other things that cut it up. By the time I got all through, I think in those days I used to get…

would come out. I never worried about what was in the contract. So it finally got up where I got — I was what they called in those days a flat artist. In other words, I used to go in, they’d pay the cost of my musicians and singers, which was a big item you know — well in those days it wasn’t that big, now it is — it was like, if you’re talking numbers, an album, a total album, musicians and singers, the first albums I did in 1956 I would say maybe $15,000, $12 or $15,000.
